title: Best Exercises for Knee Arthritis: A Simple Home Plan
metaDescription: Simple home exercises for knee arthritis: sit-to-stand, step-ups and leg raises, how often to do them, and what to avoid. Build muscle, ease pain.
intro: Exercise is one of the best treatments for knee arthritis. It strengthens the muscles that hold your knee steady, eases pain and helps you move better. Start gently once your pain is calmer, build up slowly, and do not push through sharp pain.

sections.heading: Do exercises really help knee arthritis?
sections.body: Yes. A large Cochrane review found that exercise probably reduces knee pain and improves movement, though the gain can be modest, which is why regular practice matters. The NHS and NICE both place exercise at the centre of treatment.

sections.heading: When should I start exercises?
sections.body: Usually once pain has eased with medicines. If the knee is very sore, we settle it first and then begin. Starting too hard can flare it up, so begin gently.

sections.heading: What are three simple exercises?
sections.body: Versus Arthritis suggests these to start with. Do them slowly, with control, and stop if the pain becomes sharp.
bullets: Sit-to-stand: stand from a firm chair and lower slowly.
Step-ups: step up and down on a low step, holding on.
Straight-leg raises: lie down and lift your straight leg a short way, then lower slowly.

sections.heading: How much should I do?
sections.body: Start with a few repetitions once or twice a day and build up slowly as it gets easier. A physiotherapist can set the exact numbers for you. The NHS aims for about 150 minutes of moderate activity each week, plus strengthening exercises on two or more days.

sections.heading: Which general activities are good for the knees?
sections.body: Swimming, water exercise, brisk walking, cycling, yoga, tai chi and Pilates are all suggested by Versus Arthritis because they are kind to the joints and build strength and fitness.

sections.heading: What if exercise hurts?
sections.body: Mild aching is normal. Sharp pain, a lot of swelling the next day, or a knee that gives way means you did too much. Cut back and tell us. The NHS warns that doing too much too fast can harm joints.

faqs.q: What is the best exercise for knee arthritis?
faqs.a: The best one is the one you will do regularly. Sit-to-stand, step-ups and leg raises are a good start, plus walking, cycling or swimming.

faqs.q: Can exercise make knee arthritis worse?
faqs.a: The right exercise, built up gradually, does not. Not moving usually makes stiffness and pain worse.

faqs.q: Is squatting bad for knee arthritis?
faqs.a: If squats hurt, reduce the depth. A physiotherapist can show a comfortable version.
Many people notice some change within weeks, but steady practice over months matters.
NICE says supervised exercise can help. A few sessions to set the right programme is worthwhile, then you continue at home.

faqs.q: Can I exercise with both knees affected?
faqs.a: Yes, with exercises matched to your pain. Water-based exercise can be easier.
